idiom_name: Enumerator::Lazy chains plus block-scoped streaming IO (File.open with a block, IO#read/each_line)
implementation_notes: Ruby splits the pattern between a lazy pipeline and a block-scoped resource: Enumerator::Lazy builds a chain of operations that is not evaluated until a non-lazy method (first, force, to_a) forces it, so the expensive stage runs once per demanded element, while File.open with a block, Socket and the enumerable IO methods (each, each_line, read(n), pread) acquire the handle first and the content only as it is read. Blocks double as the release mechanism: an object opened inside the block is closed when the block exits, even on exceptions, which keeps the staged release in one place. A hand-written plan is still justified when the expensive part must be shared or memoized, because Lazy re-evaluates on every traversal and caches nothing, or when stages must be coordinated across threads.
code_sketch:
File.open("pack.bin", "rb") do |io|     # stage 1: descriptor, released at block exit
  index = Pack.read_index(io)             # cheap, self-describing first part
  io.seek(index.payload_offset)           # stage 2 starts only when it is needed
  while (chunk = io.read(64 * 1024))
    sink << chunk                         # bounded read, proportional to consumption
  end
end
pitfalls: Enumerator::Lazy does not memoize: each traversal re-runs the upstream pipeline, so an expensive deferred stage is paid again unless the result is forced and stored or shared through a holder.

GC-based finalization is not release: an IO or socket that is only closed when collected keeps the expensive stage open, so the blocking forms (File.open with a block, ensure) are the deterministic choice.
The provider must outlive the staged reads: a handle closed by another thread or a connection dropped between stages surfaces as IOError/Errno in the middle of the enumeration.
An exception escaping mid-traversal leaves the partially consumed enumerator holding the file and the last read position, so a retry resumes where it stopped unless the handle is re-opened.
force/to_a on a lazy enumerator is a full acquisition; calling it for a convenient return value silently destroys the staging.
